# Adaptive laboratory evolution of Escherichia coli W enhances gamma-aminobutyric acid production using glycerol as the carbon source ![](images/1914259fe9d7377aecc84474723a9c9d2768455f3f249068feff1c1f819469da.jpg) Kangsan Kim a, Chen Yuan Hou b, Donghui Choe a, Minjeong Kang , Suhyung Cho Bong Hyun Sung c, Dae-Hee Lee c, Seung-Goo Lee c, Taek Jin Kang \*, Byung-Kwan Cho a,\* a Department of Biological Sciences and KI for the BioCentury, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Daejeon, 34141, Republic of Korea b Department of Chemical and Biochemical Engineering, Dongguk University-Seoul, Seoul, 04620, Republic of Korea c Synthetic Biology & Bioengineering Research Center, Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology, Daejeon, 34141, Republic of Korea ## A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Escherichia coli W Glycerol Adaptive laboratory evolution Gamma-aminobutyric acid Metabolic engineering ## A B S T R A C T The microbial conversion of glycerol into value-added commodity products has emerged as an attractive means to meet the demands of biosustainability. However, glycerol is a non-preferential carbon source for productive fermentation because of its low energy density. We employed evolutionary and metabolic engineering in tandem to construct an Escherichia coli strain with improved GABA production using glycerol as the feedstock carbon. Adaptive evolution of E. coli W under glycerol-limited conditions for 1300 generations harnessed an adapted strain with a metabolic system optimized for glycerol utilization. Mutation profiling, enzyme kinetic assays, and transcriptome analysis of the adapted strain allowed us to decipher the basis of glycerol adaptation at the molecular level. Importantly, increased substrate influx mediated by the mutant glpK and modulation of intracellular cAMP levels were the key drivers of improved fitness in the glycerol-limited condition. Leveraging the enhanced capability of glycerol utilization in the strain, we constructed a GABA-producing E. coli W-derivative with superior GABA production compared to the wild-type. Furthermore, rationally designed inactivation of the non-essential metabolic genes, including ackA, mgsA, and gabT, in the glycerol-adapted strain improved the final GABA titer and specific productivity by 3.9- and 4.3-fold, respectively, compared with the wild-type. ## 1. Introduction In parallel with the rapid growth of the biofuel market, increasing amounts of glycerol, which accounts for nearly 10% (v/v) of the total biodiesel products, are generated as byproducts (Da Silva et al., 2009; Mu et al., 2006). The excess glycerol made available from biodiesel transesterification has led to a dramatic decrease in the market cost of glycerol (Dharmadi et al., 2006), making it an economically attractive feedstock carbon. As many microbes utilize glycerol as their sole carbon source, numerous studies have focused on the microbial conversion of this renewable feedstock into value-added products (Da Silva et al., 2009). Escherichia coli W is one of the many microbes that utilize glycerol as their sole carbon source. It is also an emerging strain for industrial-scale production owing to its high tolerance to environmental stress and low acetate production without tight sugar control (Alterthum and Ingram, 1989; Monk et al., 2016). As one of the fastest-growing strains among commercial E. coli (Archer et al., 2011), it is thought to be an ideal platform strain for producing desired metabolites that are often generated in a growth-coupled manner. Previously, it was demonstrated that E. coli W, W3110, and BL21 (DE3) exhibited some of the highest production of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), using glycerol as the feedstock carbon (Hou and Kang, 2018). However, the absence of optimization schemes, such as metabolic engineering, to maximize GABA production requires additional engineering efforts to evaluate further the potential of GABA production by E. coli W. GABA has attracted considerable interest because of its multifunctional role in pharmaceuticals, food additives, and the synthesis of biodegradable polymers (Abdou et al., 2006; Kanjee and Houry, 2013; Park et al., 2013). It is a natural, non-proteinogenic amino acid that can be naturally produced from L-glutamate by the enzyme glutamate decarboxylase (GAD). In bacterial cells, GABA is a byproduct of an acid-resistant system that plays an important role in buffering the cells against low pH (Kanjee and Houry, 2013). Considering the value-added mid-exponential growth phase to select for the fastest growing progeny, characterized by a gradual decrease in the estimated doubling time as a function of accumulated generations (Fig. 1B). We isolated a single clone (CY02) for downstream analysis and application from the fittest end-point lineage. The specific growth rate of CY02 in the minimal glycerol medium improved by nearly 40% compared with the wild-type $( \mathrm { f r o m } 0 . 6 7 \pm 0 . 0 3 / \mathrm { h r } \mathrm { t o } 0 . 9 4 \pm 0 . 0 1 / \mathrm { h r } ) _ { \mathrm { \Omega } }$ , and was similar to that of the parental strain grown in the minimal glucose medium $( 0 . 8 7 \pm 0 . 0 4 / \mathrm { { h r } ; }$ Fig. 1C). The adaptive increase in the growth rate of the glycerol-evolved E. coli W was less dramatic than that of E. coli K-12 MG1655, which experienced a more than 2-fold increase in the growth rate between 700 and 1000 generations of glycerol ALE (Fong et al., 2005; Ibarra et al., 2002; Kang et al., 2019). Nonetheless, the final specific growth rate observed in the adapted single clone was comparable with the specific growth rate of the wild-type E. coli W in M9 supplemented with glucose, a substrate metabolically favored by many E. coli strains. However, the measured fitness in the minimal glucose medium was negligible compared with that of the wild-type, implying the adaptive changes in CY02 were rewired specifically to glycerol utilization. To assess changes in glycerol utilization in the evolved strain, we measured glycerol consumption rates of the parental strain and CY02 in the minimal glycerol medium. As expected, a significant increase in the glycerol consumption rate was observed in CY02 compared with the parental strain (Fig. 1D), highlighting that the fitness improvement observed in the minimal glycerol medium was ascribed primarily to enhanced glycerol utilization. Together, these results indicate that the 1300 generations of ALE optimized cell growth in the minimal glycerol medium. ## 2.2. Identification of causal mutations during glycerol adaptation Accumulation of beneficial mutations in the course of ALE is responsible for the adaptation and improved fitness of the strain (Applebee et al., 2011; Cheng et al., 2014; Herring et al., 2006; Kang et al., 2019). To pinpoint the causal mutations underlying fitness improvement, we performed whole-genome resequencing of the parental strain, the end-point population, and CY02. Ninety-three genomic mutations were found in the adaptively evolved population, and 89 genomic mutations were mapped to CY02. Among them, the background mutations found in the parental E. coli W strain cultured in our laboratory (genetic sequence in conflict with the reference genome NC\_017635.1) were omitted from the analysis. Thus, we detected 30 and 28 new mutations in the ALE population and the single clone CY02, respectively. To identify the causal mutations that contributed to improved fitness, we focused on the shared mutations between the two groups (Table 1 and Fig. S1). Some of the notable mutations included disabling mutations (either frame-shifts or nonsense mutations) in ptsP (phosphoenolpyruvate protein phosphotransferase), rsfS (ribosomal silencing factor), or mglC (galactoside transporter system permease). Single nucleotide variations (SNVs) included glpK (glycerol kinase) and crp (global transcriptional regulator CRP) (Table 1). Regarding genes with disabling mutations, $p t s P$ encodes a component of the nitrogen phosphotransferase system in E. coli. The inactivation of ptsP was previously shown to enhance acetate assimilation in E. coli (Hara et al., 2009), which is thought to be caused by increased cellular ATP synthesis in the ptsP deletion mutant (Hara et al., 2009). The recurrence of similar inactivating mutations in ptsP in different ALEs suggests causality of the $p t s P$ mutants in fitness improvement (Kang et al., 2019; Phaneuf et al., 2019; Sandberg et al., 2017; Wannier et al., 2018). However, counterintuitively, the pstP deletion mutant exhibited fitness retardation compared with the wild-type in acetate-limited culture conditions (Gu et al., 2019), leaving the role of the ptsP frame-shift mutation in strain fitness rather elusive. However, rsfS suffered a nonsense mutation in the 7th codon, possibly rendering the protein prematurely terminated. RsfS is thought to play a role in translation inhibition during the stationary phase or under suboptimal growth conditions. Its knockout mutant exhibits impaired viability in the stationary phase or when transferred from a nutritionally rich to poor medium (Hauser et al., 2012). However, given the relatively low frequency of rsfS mutants in ALE (Phaneuf et al., 2019), it is difficult to assume the implications of RsfS inactivation in adaptation. Likewise, the lack of relevant references on mglC mutants makes it difficult to infer the evolutionary advantage of the mglC mutant found in this study. In fact, the specific growth rate of the reverse-engineered mglC mutant remained the same as that of the wild-type (Fig. S2), suggesting that the mglC mutant is a “hitchhiker mutation” that confers no apparent advantage in glycerol adaptation. Therefore, we assumed that the mutants of glpK and crp, which were recurrently mutated under glycerol and nutrient limitation conditions, were the key mutations contributing to glycerol adaptation in E. coli W. Mutations in glpK are highly recurrent in ALE performed in minimal glycerol media (Cheng et al., 2014; Fong et al., 2005; Herring et al., 2006; Kang et al., 2019). As the rate-limiting factor of the glycerol utilization process in E. coli (Zwaig et al., 1970), the glpK mutants are “specialist mutations” that confer fitness advantages under culture conditions supplemented with glycerol as the sole carbon source. Often, glpK mutants exhibit significantly reduced or diminished sensitivity towards inhibitory effects of fructose 1,6-bisphosphate (FBP) and $\mathrm { I I A } ^ { \mathrm { { \dot { G } l c } } } -$ mediated allosteric inhibition, thereby allowing higher glycerol influx into the cell (Applebee et al., 2011; Freedberg et al., 1971; Novotny et al., 1985; Postma et al., 1984; Zwaig and Lin, 1966). The glpK mutant isolated in this study harbors a missense mutation at the FBP binding site (Thr235Met; hereafter $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } } ) _ { \mathrm { : } }$ , suggesting altered interaction with FBP inhibitor. Similarly, SNVs in crp are also frequently observed in ALE conducted under nutrient-limited conditions, signifying an adaptive nature of crp mutants (Fong et al., 2005; Kang et al., 2019; Sievert et al., 2017; Wannier et al., 2018). As the master regulator of more than 500 genes in E. coli, crp mutants have been proposed to enhance host fitness via altered binding dynamics with cAMP and the target DNA domain or by interacting with RNA polymerase activating domains (Frendorf et al., 2019). In particular, several mutations in the cAMP binding site of crp have been reported to allow utilization of non-PTS carbon sources, even in the absence of cAMP (Frendorf et al., 2019). However, the crp mutation identified in this study was positioned towards the C-terminus (R209H; hereafter $c r p ^ { \mathrm { m } } )$ . In this regard, we sought to investigate whether $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ and $c r p ^ { \mathrm { { m } } }$ found in CY02 recapitulate their beneficial effects on strain fitness. ## 2.3. Mutation on glpK increases carbon uptake by preventing the allosteric inhibition by fructose $^ { 1 , 6 }$ bis-phosphate First, we measured the specific growth rates and glycerol consumption rates of the E. coli W parental strain, causative mutants, and CY02 in a minimal glycerol medium. To this end, single mutants of $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ and $c r p ^ { \mathrm { { m } } }$ and a strain harboring both mutations $( g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } } c r p ^ { \mathrm { m } } )$ were reverseengineered using the λ-Red recombinase-mediated method (Datsenko and Wanner, 2000). Significant increases in specific growth rates were observed in $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ (1.45-fold; independent t-test p-value $< ~ 0 . 0 2 2 )$ $g { l p } K ^ { \mathrm { m } } c { r p } ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ (1.56-fold; $\mathbf { p } ~ = ~ 0 . 0 3 7 )$ , and CY02 (1.63-fold; p-value = 0.009). However, the change in $c r p ^ { \mathrm { { m } } }$ was not significant (Fig. 2A). Similarly, the specific glycerol uptake rate (GUR) increased significantly in the glpKm-harboring strains (1.78-fold; $\mathbf { p } \mathbf { - } \mathbf { v a l u e } = 0 . 0 2$ for $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } } ,$ 1.70-fold; p-value = 0.016 for $g { l p } K ^ { \mathrm { m } } c { r p } ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ , and 1.60-fold; p-value = 0.036 for CY02), but not in $c r p ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ (Fig. 2B). These results indicated that, consistent with previous findings, $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ alone accounts for a substantial portion of the fitness improvement in E. coli W under glycerol-limitation conditions. The significant increase in GUR observed among $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ harboring strains also suggests that the increased carbon uptake is the primary driver of improved fitness. However, although it appeared that $c r p ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ was inversely correlated with GUR while positively contributing to specific growth rates, the apparent lack of statistical significance leaves the fitness correlates of $c r p ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ elusive. Next, we tested the enzyme kinetics of the mutant GlpK $\mathrm { ( G l p K ^ { m } ) }$ to obtain insights into the observed fitness improvement in the minimal glycerol medium. Among 502 amino acids comprising GlpK in E. coli, Gly 233, Gly 234, and Arg 236 are known to form an exposed loop that offers a binding site for its allosteric inhibitor FBP (Anderson et al., 2007; Ormo et al., 1998). As our mutation was located within the two glycine-arginine loops (Fig. S3A), we reasoned that the interaction between GlpK and FBP would be altered. To examine changes in enzymatic properties, wild-type GlpK (GlpKw) from the parental strain and $\mathrm { G l p K ^ { m } }$ from CY02 were overexpressed and purified (Fig. S3B). The catalytic activity $\left( \mathrm { V } _ { 0 } / \mathrm { V } _ { \mathrm { m a x } } \right)$ of $\mathrm { { G l p K } ^ { m } }$ did not differ from that of the wild-type. However, although the specific activity of $\mathrm { G l p K } ^ { \mathrm { w } }$ decreased with increasing FBP concentration, it remained constant in $\mathrm { { G l p K } ^ { m } }$ at all concentrations tested, indicating a loss of affinity towards FBP (Fig. 2C and D and Table 2). This is consistent with the observation that the inhibitory effect imparted by FBP was diminished in the GlpK Arg236Ala mutant (Ormo et al., 1998). In this regard, it appeared that the increased fitness observed in $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } } .$ -harboring strains in minimal glycerol medium was attributable to the changes in enzymatic regulatory mechanisms (Applebee et al., 2011; Zwaig et al., 1970). In addition to assessing the effects of mutations on strain fitness, we also examined changes in cellular signaling and gene expression. It has been documented that intracellular cAMP levels are reduced in the presence of glpK mutations that are either insensitive to FBP or incapable of tetramerization (Applebee et al., 2011). Reduced intracellular cAMP downregulates the expression of the CRP-cAMP-sensitive glpFK operon, leading to decreased glpK expression. Such regulation occurs through the repression of adenylate cyclase elicited by the accumulation of glycerol-3-phosphate (G3P), the product of GlpK, thereby lowering the intracellular cAMP (Eppler et al., 2002) (Fig. 3A). One plausible explanation for the biological significance of G3P-mediated catabolite repression is that cAMP reduction is part of an autoregulatory mechanism to buffer the excessive accumulation of methylglyoxal, an intermediate of glycerol metabolism that is toxic above a certain threshold (Applebee et al., 2011; Booth, 2005; Freedberg et al., 1971). This notion could explain the highly pronounced G3P-induced catabolite repression among the GlpK mutants that enhance glycerol uptake (Applebee et al., 2011). To test whether E. coli W recapitulates the transcriptomic and biochemical shifts following glycerol adaptation, we first measured intracellular cAMP levels of the parental strain, each single and double mutant, and CY02 during the exponential phase. As expected, the intracellular cAMP levels in the reverse-engineered strains harboring the $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ mutation dramatically decreased by nearly 98% of that measured in the wild-type (Fig. 3B), this is far lower than that documented for the MG1655 strain (between 30% and 50% of the wild-type) (Applebee et al., 2011; Cheng et al., 2014). Despite harboring the identical glpK mutation $( g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } } )$ , the intracellular cAMP in CY02 was approximately 10-fold higher (20% of the wild-type) than that of the $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ single mutant. This suggests that the low intracellular cAMP levels observed in the $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ single and double mutants were maladaptive. The significant reduction in the $c r p ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ single mutant, which retained only 36% of the cAMP measured in the wild-type, was unanticipated (Fig. 3B). The $c r p ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ found in this study was initially presumed to have a null effect on strain fitness because the mutation was positioned toward the C-terminal end (Arg209His). Although it is unclear how the $c r p ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ mutant exerted such a change in the intracellular cAMP level, the presence of a DNA-binding domain in the vicinity of Arg209His allowed us to speculate that $\mathrm { C R P ^ { m } }$ may differ from the wild-type in DNA-binding interactions. Consistent with the changes in the intracellular cAMP abundance, the comparison of glpK mRNA transcript abundance measured using RT-qPCR between the strains revealed a concurrent decline in all mutants and the evolved strain (Fig. S4). The measured glpK expression of the $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ -harboring strains, including CY02, ranged between 3% and 6% compared to that of the wild-type, which was within the range of the relative expression level of the mutant glpK, as reported previously (Applebee et al., 2011). The relative expression of glpK in $c r p ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ background was approximately 22% that of the wild-type. The expression in the double mutant $( g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } } c r p ^ { \mathrm { m } } )$ was less than half that in the $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ single mutant, which appeared to indicate the presence of $c r p ^ { \mathrm { { m } } } .$ -mediated expression regulation. Currently, it is predicted that CRP governs the expression of approximately 11.6% of all genes in E. coli (535 out of 4629 genes) as inferred from RegulonDB (Santos-Zavaleta et al., 2019). Therefore, it is speculated that the drastic change in intracellular cAMP, which forms a complex with the apo-CRP dimer to mediate gene expression regulation, would translate to an extensive rewiring of the cellular transcriptome (Sharma et al., 2009). To gain insight into genome-wide transcriptome changes in response to glycerol adaptation, we performed RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) on the wild-type and CY02 strains harvested during exponential growth in minimal glycerol medium. An average of 79.6% and 77.3% of the total reads were mapped to the wild-type and CY02 strain, respectively, with a high correlation among the biological triplicates (Fig. S5). A total of 640 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using DESeq2 (Love et al., 2014). Among them, 149 genes were upregulated, and 491 genes were downregulated in the CY02 strain compared to that of the parental strain (Supplementary Table S1 and Fig. S6). We found that 181 genes of the DEGs were regulated by CRP (Santos-Zavaleta et al., 2019). The percentage of the CRP regulons differentially expressed between the wild-type and CY02 outweighed the total frequency of the CRP regulon in the E. coli genome (\~12%) by more than 2-fold, signifying the impact of the change in intracellular cAMP level, and possibly the adaptive changes in glycerol utilization. The differentially expressed CRP regulons consisted of 157 positively regulated, 14 negatively regulated, eight ambiguous, and two unknown genes (Supplementary Table S1). Therefore, we assumed that any changes in the expression profile of these CRP regulons between the wild-type and cAMP-depleted CY02 would indicate the impact of the differences in intracellular cAMP levels. Indeed, 148 out of 157 positively regulated genes were significantly downregulated in CY02 compared with that of the wild-type, an effect that manifested as the result of reduced intracellular cAMP. However, such changes in gene expression were not as evident in the negatively regulated genes, with only five out of 14 upregulated in CY02 (Supplementary Table S1). Together, these results appeared to corroborate the expected transcriptomic changes in response to reduced intracellular cAMP levels. ## 2.5. Improved glycerol utilization leads to increased acetate overflow We assessed the changes in transcriptomic responses to glycerol adaptation in the core metabolic pathways of E. coli W (Fig. 4A and Supplementary Table S2). First, the expression of genes in the lower glycolytic pathway was significantly upregulated in the CY02 compared with the wild-type strain, reflecting the cellular response to the increased influx of the glycolytic substrate. Next, an overall decline in the expression of genes was observed in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, respiratory proteins, and ATP synthases in CY02. In contrast, the expression of pta and ackA increased significantly, suggesting a pronounced involvement of the fermentation pathway in energy biogenesis in CY02 (Fig. 4A and Supplementary Table S2). The transcriptome data appeared to reflect the “aerobic acetate overflow,” characterized by excess acetate production in fast-growing, aerobically cultured microbes (Wolfe, 2005). It has been reported that this phenomenon results from an excess influx of glycolytic substrates, requiring more respiratory chain proteins for ATP generation via respiration, thereby imposing a higher proteomic cost for ATP generation via respiration than by fermentation. Under such circumstances, cells dissipate the excess redox potential in glycolytic substrates via overflow pathways, which are more “proteome-effective” when the cellular proteomic space is limiting (Basan et al., 2015; Zeng and Yang, 2019). It is also worth noting that acs, which encodes acetyl-CoA synthetase, was significantly downregulated in CY02. To test whether the transcriptomic changes outlined above translate into increased acetate availability in the spent medium, we determined the acetate secretion rate of CY02 and the wild-type strain during exponential growth. The results showed that whereas the availability of acetate in the wild-type culture medium was insufficient for accurate determination of secretion rate, it was far above the detection limit in CY02, indicating increased acetate overflow (Fig. 4B). acs is part of the CRP-cAMP regulon. The reduction of intracellular cAMP induced by auto-catabolite repression triggered through the high G3P levels in glpK mutants leads to downregulation of acs (Applebee et al., 2011; Cheng et al., 2014). To test whether the overflow observed in CY02 is attributable to glpK , we measured the acetate production rates in mutants with $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } } , c r p ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ , or $g { l p } K ^ { \mathrm { m } } c { r p } ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ genetic backgrounds. Indeed, mutants harboring $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ exhibited increased acetate production rates comparable to CY02 (Fig. 4B). Interestingly, despite the apparent reduction in the measured cAMP level in $c r p ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ , the acetate production rate was not determinable. This suggests that cAMP-CRP regulation alone does not fully account for acetate overflow in E. coli (Basan et al., 2015). Instead, acetate overflow in $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ -containing mutants results from combined actions between the $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ -mediated auto-catabolite repression, which induces downregulation of acs and activates a more proteomically efficient energy generation pathway, pta and ackA. ## 2.6. GABA production in E. coli W Taking advantage of the improved glycerol uptake and utilization observed in the glycerol-evolved E. coli $\mathsf { W } ,$ we examined whether such improvements translated into superior commodity metabolite production from glycerol. Previously, it was demonstrated that E. coli W exhibited some of the highest GABA production levels under glycerol limitation among other E. coli strains, including W3110, DH5α, and BL21 (DE3) (Hou and Kang, 2018). To test whether ALE leads to improved GABA production, we used a variant of glutamate decarboxylase B (mtGAD) in the strain. Unlike its wild-type counterpart, the variant is catalytically active even at physiological pH, making it the enzyme of choice for GABA production via bacterial fermentation (Choi et al., 2015; Hou and Kang, 2018; Thu Ho et al., 2013). The mutant gene is under the control of an inducible promoter PLtetQ-1, but the lack of a cognate repressor in the E. coli W genome allowed constitutive expression of mtGAD. The GABA expression cassette was inserted into the chromosome, precluding the use of antibiotic markers during cell culture. The measurement of GABA production in the E. coli W wild-type and CY02 in M9 glycerol minimal medium revealed that the differences in the final GABA concentration were negligible $( 0 . 0 6 \pm 0 . 0 1$ and 0.06 ± 0.01 g/L for wild-type and CY02, respectively). There are few related but mutually exclusive reasons that offer plausible explanations for this observation. First, cells display “inefficient growth” in the presence of excess carbon intake under carbon-limited conditions, which is characterized by cells allocating much of the substrate input in generating excess energy than in biomass (Basan et al., 2015; Russell and Cook, 1995). This has also been proven to be true for E. coli harboring the glpK mutants (Basan et al., 2015) and appears to be the case for CY02, as seen through the superfluous acetate overflow. Under such circumstances, cells are less efficient in generating biomass, thereby imposing constraints on biomass formation, such as heterologous protein expression and plasmid acquisition (el-Mansi and Holms, 1989; Prensky et al., 2021). Additionally, the cost of amino acid biosynthesis is highly dependent on the “metabolic network.” The underlying cost of production is proportional to the number of reactions required to synthesize amino acids from the input substrate (Waschina et al., 2016). Given that L-glutamate is converted from α-ketoglutarate in the TCA cycle, conversion of the glycolytic substrate glycerol into L-glutamate incurs some of the highest metabolic costs (Waschina et al., 2016). Although 50 mg/L of yeast extract was present in the minimal medium used for GABA production, it might not have been sufficient to meet the cellular L-glutamate demands. Lastly, together with the growth inefficiency and the high biosynthetic cost of L-glutamate from glycerol, the amount of glycerol supplemented in the medium (0.2% v/v) can be a limiting factor in the growth-coupled production of GABA under nutrient limitation. Several studies have supplemented at least 10 g/L (equivalent to 1%) of feedstock carbons (i.e., glucose) in the culture medium to facilitate GABA production (Choi et al., 2015; Im et al., 2020; Le Vo et al., 2012, 2013; Luo et al., 2021; Soma et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2017). Together, we reasoned that these compounding factors in a minimal glycerol medium might have overshadowed the effect of enhanced glycerol uptake and utilization in CY02 on GABA production. Following approaches were used to optimize GABA production: previously, it has been demonstrated that growth inefficiency can be restored upon supplementation with amino acids, resulting in a more efficient substrate-to-biomass conversion (Prensky et al., 2021; Russell and Cook, 1995; Waschina et al., 2016). Therefore, we used amino acid-rich Luria Bertani (LB) medium supplemented with glycerol as the sole carbon source. We also determined the optimal glycerol concentration for cell culture by using growth rate as a proxy, assuming that GABA production is growth-coupled. The highest specific growth rates were observed in the culture medium containing 2% glycerol (v/v) in the wild-type and $g l p K ^ { m } .$ -containing mutants (Fig. S7). Next, the final GABA concentration was measured for the wild-type, $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } } , \ c r p ^ { \mathrm { m } } ;$ $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } } c r p ^ { \mathrm { m } } ;$ , and CY02 cultured in $\mathrm { L B } + 2 \% ( \mathrm { v / v } )$ glycerol medium from the stationary phase of growth. GABA concentration measured at the stationary phase was significantly higher across the mutants harboring $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ compared with the wild-type, suggesting that medium composition is integral for efficient GABA production $( 0 . 0 5 \pm 0 . 0 1 , 0 . 0 6 \pm 0 . 0 0 _ { \hphantom { 0 } }$ $0 . 0 7 \pm 0 . 0 0 , 0 . 0 7 \pm 0 . 0 0$ , and $0 . 1 7 \pm 0 . 0 1 { \bf g } / \mathrm { L }$ in wild-type, $c r p ^ { \mathrm { m } } , g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } } c r p ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ , and CY02, respectively). Notably, the most significant increase in GABA production was observed in CY02, signifying that global optimization of a metabolic pathway, in addition to superior substrate uptake, is pivotal for enhancing target metabolite production in microbial systems. To assess the time-course changes in the GABA titer and productivity in the wild-type and CY02, we measured GABA concentration from the spent medium for over 24 h. First, CY02 maintained a higher growth rate than the wild-type strain in the LB-based medium (Fig. 5A). The maximum titer and productivity in the wild-type was $0 . 1 5 \pm 0 . 0 1 ~ \mathbf { g } / \mathrm { L }$ and $0 . 0 3 \pm 0 . 0 1 \mathrm { g / L / h r } ,$ respectively, both of which increased by nearly 2.6-fold following $\mathrm { A L E } \ ( 0 . 3 9 \pm 0 . 0 3 \ \mathrm { g / L }$ and $0 . 0 8 ~ \pm ~ 0 . 0 1$ g/L/hr) (Fig. 5B). The difference in the total amount of glycerol consumed was negligible, suggesting that the improved GABA production in CY02 is likely ascribed to the improved metabolic efficiency and biomass yield following adaptive evolution (Cheng et al., 2014). ## 2.7. Metabolic engineering of E. coli W to improve GABA production As an excessive substrate input is wired to energy generation in the form of acetate overflow in CY02, we tested whether we could re-direct this metabolic flux to GABA production. To meet this objective, we constructed several knockout mutants shown to enhance GABA production or glycerol tolerance in E. coli. These included ackA (acetate kinase), mgsA (methylglyoxal synthase), and gabT (4-aminobutyrate aminotransferase) (Fig. 6A). Of the many knockout targets, these three were chosen for the following reasons: first, owing to the highly profuse acetate overflow seen in CY02, we decided that ackA inactivation would re-route excess carbons that are otherwise excreted into the culture medium. ackA is one of many genes associated with mixed-acid fermentation pathways that are routinely targeted for metabolic engineering, including GABA production (Pham et al., 2015, 2016). Further, it was reported that the presence of glpK mutants that enhance glycerol uptake $( \mathrm { i . e . , }$ insensitive to FBP-mediated inhibition) could lead to the build-up of methylglyoxal, an intermediate of glycerol metabolism, up to a cytotoxic level (Freedberg et al., 1971). One way to curb the potentially damaging effects of methylglyoxal accumulation is to inactivate mgsA, which encodes methylglyoxal synthase that catalyzes the conversion of DHAP to methylglyoxal (Mazumdar et al., 2013). MgsA is also involved in an intermediate pathway that yields lactate enantiomers in E. coli, an auxiliary pathway that can improve target metabolite production upon inactivation (Mazumdar et al., 2013). Finally, gabT constitutes a GABA shunt pathway that feeds GABA back into the TCA cycle via a two-step reaction. For this reason, deletion of gabT is a common practice to improve GABA production in bacteria (Im et al., 2020; Le Vo et al., 2012, 2013; Luo et al., 2021; Pham et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2017). Therefore, we deleted each single and all target genes in CY02, yielding three single knockouts and a triple knockout strain denoted as CY02\_ΔackA, CY02\_ΔgabT, CY02\_ΔmgsA, and CY02\_TKO (Fig. 6A). The time-course measurement of growth rate and GABA production in each single and triple knockout strain showed that the gene knockout did not affect cell growth rate, although strains with ΔackA (CY02\_ΔackA, CY02\_ΔgabTΔackA, CY02\_ ΔmgsAΔackA and CY02\_TKO) exhibited a prolonged lag phase growth (Fig. 6B; Fig. S8A). However, the results of GABA production in the CY02 derivatives were counterintuitive. Although the final GABA titer in all single knockout strains was lower than that of the wild-type, it was significantly higher in the double and the triple knockout derivatives (Fig. 6C; Fig. S8B). Variations in GABA production was seen in the double knockout derivatives. The final GABA titers of ΔgabTΔackA, and ΔgabTΔmgsA $( 0 . 4 6 \pm 0 . 0 2$ and 0.45 ± 0.01 g/L respectively; Fig. S8B), were higher than CY02 and all single knock derivatives, but were lower than the triple knockout derivative. On the other hand, while the final GABA titer in CY02\_ΔmgsAΔackA $( 0 . 3 7 \pm 0 . 0 4 \ : \mathrm { g / L } )$ was higher than the two single knockout mutants – CY02\_ΔackA and CY02\_ ΔmgsA, it remained lower compared to CY02 and CY02\_ΔgabT single knockout. This suggested that deletion of gabT gene, which is associated with GABA shunt pathway, was important for improving GABA production in the evolved strain. The deletion of three target genes resulted in a further increase in the GABA titer and productivity by 1.5- and 1.6-fold, respectively (Table 3). To assess whether the observed effects of gene deletions on GABA production was an intrinsic feature of E. coli W, we also measured GABA production in knockout derivatives of the wild-type lacZ:mtGAD strain (Fig. 6D and E; Figs. S8C and D). The results suggested that the deletion of ackA, gabT, and mgsA, in general, leads to lower GABA production compared to that of the wild-type. However, the effect of the double and the triple knockout in CY02 was not observed in the wild-type, suggesting that the improved GABA production in CY02 double and triple knockouts was attributable to the rewired metabolic network. As genetic mutations are the key variables that underlie the phenotypic differences between the wild-type and CY02, the varied response to the multi-gene knockouts is seemingly ascribable to the background effect imparted by the mutations acquired in the course of evolution (Mullis et al., 2018). The prevalence of epistatic interactions in the genetic network translates to the idea that any changes in the genetic background (or mutations) may potentially alter the phenotypic outcome of genetic changes acquired later. In this case, the inactivation of the three genes (ackA, mgsA, and gabT) together elicited unknown epistatic interactions in the CY02 mutational background, leading to improved GABA production. Discussion It has been previously shown that the metabolic network in wild-type E. coli strains is not optimized for glycerol utilization and that strain fitness under glycerol limitation can be further improved through adaptive evolution experiments (Cheng et al., 2014; Herring et al., 2006; Ibarra et al., 2002; Kang et al., 2019). ALE is a robust top-down approach that harnesses microbes with desired characteristics. This approach exploits the innate ability of microbes to rapidly adapt to new environments and is now widely used across a broad spectrum of applications, including, but not limited to, strain development and fitness optimization (Dragosits and Mattanovich, 2013; Portnoy et al., 2011). In this study, a novel glpK mutation was identified, which accounted for more than 90% of the fitness increase in CY02. We also leveraged ALE to allow efficient utilization of non-preferential carbon glycerol in a fast-growing E. coli strain W. We observed a significant fitness increase in E. coli W harboring a non-synonymous nucleotide substitution in glpK, which is in keeping with previous findings in E. coli (Applebee et al., 2011). Although the amino acid change in the glpKm (GlpK T235M) identified in this study has not been previously isolated, the mutation in the vicinity of the FBP-binding position led us to infer the mechanistic basis of glpKm. With kinetic experiments to validate the prediction that the increased glycerol uptake observed in CY02 was attributable to FBP-insensitive GlpKm. The $g l p K ^ { \mathrm { m } }$ also showed the hallmarks of glpK mutants, including the auto-regulation of intracellular cAMP levels arising from increased glycerol influx, downregulation of glpK gene expression, and excessive acetate overflow (Applebee et al., 2011; Cheng et al., 2014). Together, these results highlighted the universality of glpK mutant in glycerol adaptation in different E. coli strains. The productivity and titer of GABA in the evolved strain CY02, along with additional metabolic engineering design, increased by 4.3- and 3.9 folds (0.13 ± 0.02 g/L/hr and 0.59 ± 0.04 g/L), respectively. Quantitively speaking, GABA production in the engineered E. coli W was not high compared to other studies. Just as other metabolites, GABA production is heavily dependent on the mode of production (bioconversion or fermentation), types of feedstock used, and with huge strain-wide variability in production. For instance, engineered E. coli (i.e. overexpression of GAD genes and gene knockouts) produced approximately 5.6 g/L of GABA in LB supplemented with monosodium glutamate (MSG) as the substrate (Le Vo et al., 2012, 2013). The titer was much lower when glucose was supplemented instead (\~1.3 g/L) (Pham et al., 2015). With bioconversion method, a staggering 313.1 g/L of GABA titer was achieved via extracellular expression of GAD gene in an extreme-rich medium (Zhao et al., 2016). In addition, natural isolates with a robust GABA production capacity, such as Lactobacillus brevis NCL912, and Lactobacillus buchneri WPZ001, were shown to achieve GABA titer of 104 and 129 g/L respectively via fermentation in MSG-supplemented rich media (Li et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2015). The primary focus of this study was to demonstrate the applicability of evolutionary and metabolic engineering in tandem for improving target metabolite production. For instance, evolutionary engineering (ALE) alone showed a 2.6-fold increase in the maximum GABA production in the $\mathrm { L B } + 2 \% ( \mathrm { v / v } )$ glycerol culture condition. Such an increase is comparable, or sometimes even better off, than other engineering attempts that utilized highly efficient carbon sources such as glucose and MSG (ranging between 1.2 and 4.6-fold increase in titer from genome engineering alone) (Im et al., 2020; Le Vo et al., 2013; Pham et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2019). With respect to bioconversion of waste, bioconversion of renewable biomass wastes, including agricultural, food, municipal waste and forest remains, into commodity products have been increasingly highlighted in the last few years due to the compelling need for sustainability (Bhatia et al., 2018). However, the use of model strain E. coli can be limited when it comes to the choice of feedstocks. Bioconversion of ‘difficult renewable wastes typically requires species of microorganisms that can efficiently degrade, utilize and convert target molecules. For example, lignocellulosic solid waste consists mainly of plant-derived cellulose hence requiring the use of microbial species with high cellulolytic activity, which is largely lacking in model E. coli strains (Sarsaiya et al., 2018). Bioconversion of waste gaseous substances into commodity also mandates the use of highly specialized bacteria, such as facultative anaerobe acetogens, that can subsist on gaseous feedstocks (Bae et al., 2021). It is expected that such forms of waste feedstocks can be a much cheaper alternative for microbial bioconversion compared with conventional feedstock carbons. In addition, the complementary benefit of a cleaner environment coupled with rapidly increasing waste generation (Kaza et al., 2018) together calls for a more efficient and cost-effective biowaste conversion technology. To this end, the development of versatile microbial host systems tailored for waste bioconversion is needed to effectively convert diverse waste sources into value-added products. ## 4. Materials and methods ## 4.1. Bacterial strains, culture conditions and primers Cells were grown in M9 minimal medium (BD, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA) supplemented with 0.2% (v/v) glycerol (Samchun Chemicals, Seoul, South Korea) or Luria Bertani (LB) medium unless stated otherwise. The growth profile in Fig. S7 was performed using the EPOCH2 plate reader (BioTek, Winnoski, VT, United States) at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ with shaking (807 rpm double orbital) for 24 h, using default 96-well configuration (110 μL of working volume). Absorbance $\mathtt { a t } \lambda = 6 0 0$ nm was measured at 10-min intervals. The resulting data output was analyzed on the Gen 5 software. The primers, bacterial strains, and plasmids used in this study are listed in Supplementary Table S3. ## 4.2. ALE and strain isolation E. coli W was cultivated in 50 mL of M9 glycerol medium in a 250 mL Erlenmeyer flat-bottom flask at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ with agitation. The batch cultures were transferred to fresh M9 glycerol medium every 12 h. Initially, the initial optical density at 600 nm $\left( \mathrm { A } _ { 6 0 0 \mathrm { n m } } \right)$ was set to 0.0008, and it was reduced to 0.0004 and, subsequently, to 0.00016 in a stepwise manner. The number of generations during ALE was calculated from the initial and final cell densities using Eq. (1): $$ { \mathrm { N u m b e r ~ o f ~ \ g e n e r a t i o n } } = \log 2 _ { 2 } { \frac { { \mathrm { F i n a l ~ \ c e l l ~ \ d e n s i t y } } } { { \mathrm { I n i t i a l ~ \ c e l l ~ \ d e n s i t y } } } }\tag{1} $$ Single clones were isolated in the M9 glycerol agar medium after ALE. A single clone was isolated for further analysis (CY02). ## 4.3. Whole-genome resequencing Genomic DNA was isolated using a Wizard Genomic DNA purification kit (Promega, Madison, WI, USA), following the manufacturer’s instructions. Cells collected by centrifugation were lysed by resuspension in Nuclei Lysis Solution and incubation at 80 ◦C for 5 min. The cell lysate was incubated at $3 7 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 30 min with 1.2 μg of RNase A (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). Proteins were precipitated using protein precipitation solution, and genomic DNA was precipitated using isopropanol and 70% $\mathbf { ( v / v ) }$ ethanol. Genomic DNA was rehydrated using Milli-Q ultrapure water (Merck, Kenilworth, NJ, USA). The resequencing library was constructed using the TruSeq DNA LT Sample Prep Kit (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA). The gDNA library was sequenced using the MiSeq Reagent Kit v2 (Illumina) in a 50-cycle single-ended reaction on the MiSeq instrument. ## 4.4. Construction of mutant strains The target genes were replaced by $\mathrm { K a n } ^ { \mathrm { R } }$ by lambda Red recombination of the parental W strain (Datsenko and Wanner, 2000) (see plasmids and primers used in mutant construction in Supplementary Table S3). The kanamycin resistance cassette was amplified from pKD13 by using PCR with homology to the target region. The recombinogenic DNA (1 μg) was introduced into electrocompetent cells containing pKD46, via electroporation on a MicroPulser (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA) at 1.8 kV in a 0.1 cm gap cuvette. A recipient was selected on LB agar containing 50 μg/mL kanamycin. The selected colonies were transformed with pCP20 to eliminate the $\mathrm { K a n } ^ { \mathrm { R } }$ marker. The temperature-sensitive plasmids were cured by incubation in LB medium at $4 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ ## 4.5. Glycerol and acetate quantification To measure glycerol and acetate in cell culture media, each strain was inoculated in 50 mL of M9 glycerol minimal medium in 250 mL Erlenmeyer flasks. After 1.5 h of incubation, 1.5 mL of the cell culture was collected at 1 h intervals during the exponential growth phase. The samples were centrifuged at $^ { 1 4 , 8 1 4 \times g }$ at $4 ~ { } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 1 min, and the supernatant was filtered using a 0.2 μm pore size cellulose acetate syringe filter (Sartorius, Gottingen, Germany). Quantification of glycerol and acetate was performed using a Cedex Bio Analyzer (Roche, Basel, Switzerland) with the Glycerol Bio Test kit and Acetate V2 Bio Test kit. The glycerol consumption and acetate secretion rates were determined as described in a previous study (Heyland et al., 2009), using the equations below: $$ r _ { \mathrm { g l y c e r o l } } = \frac { \mu } { Y _ { X _ { / _ { s } } } }\tag{2} $$ $$ r _ { \mathrm { a c e t a t e } } = { \frac { \mu } { Y _ { P _ { \tilde { \jmath } _ { X } } } } }\tag{3} $$ where μ is the specific growth rate, $\Upsilon _ { \mathbf { x } / \mathbf { s } }$ is the biomass yield of glycerol, and $\mathrm { Y } _ { \mathrm { p / x } }$ is the product yield coefficient of biomass. ## 4.6. GlpK expression and purification Wild-type and mutant glpK sequences were cloned into the pET28a (+) vector by using an In-fusion HD cloning kit (Takara, Kusatsu, Japan). The wild-type glpK sequence was amplified by PCR from the parental W, whereas the mutant glpK sequence was amplified from the glycerol-evolved single clone CY02.6 × His tags were added to the Nterminus of the expressed proteins. The isolated clone of each transformant was cultivated in 200 mL of LB with kanamycin (50 μg/mL) at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ . Protein expression was induced with 1 mM IPTG. Cells were collected and lysed in lysis buffer (20 mM pH 8.0 Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole, 1 × protease inhibitor cocktail, and 1 mg/mL lysozyme) and sonicated (30% amplitude, pulse on 3 s, off 9 s, total on time 10 min). The column was washed using a washing buffer (20 mM pH 8.0 Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, and 20 mM imidazole). The protein was eluted in elution buffer (20 mM pH 8.0 Tris-HCl, 300 mM NaCl, and 250 mM imidazole buffer). The eluted protein was dialyzed using a float-A-Lyzer G2 dialysis device (Repligen, Waltham, MA, USA) in storage buffer (50 mM pH 6.8 Tris-HCl, 200 mM NaCl, 1 mM β-mercaptoethanol, 20% (v/ v) ethylene glycol, and 2 mM glycerol in sterile water). The dialyzed proteins were monitored by SDS-PAGE. ## 4.7. Intracellular cAMP assay Sample preparation was performed as previously described (Death and Ferenci, 1994). Change in cellular cAMP level elicited by increased glycerol influx. (A) Proposed changes in glycerol metabolism, regulation, and gene expression in the presence of the GlpK mutant.
